rationale: Start with a broad gradient at moderate temperature to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. This provides a baseline for subsequent slope and temperature comparisons.

All peaks are well resolved, so halve the gradient time to reduce the time penalty and measure how the critical pairs respond to increased steepness. Keep the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed for a clean comparison.
The critical cluster responds strongly to gradient slope. An intermediate gradient should recover much of its resolution while keeping the last peak substantially earlier than in the initial run.

A slightly shallower gradient should improve the critical pair, while raising temperature may offset the longer gradient’s retention-time cost. This tests a candidate for full resolution with little or no time penalty.

The warmer run suggests that the critical pair is approaching an elution-order crossover. Test the highest temperature to seek renewed separation beyond that crossover while shortening retention, using injection 3’s gradient for comparison.

At 60 C, the previous critical cluster is resolved and only one earlier pair remains below target. Lengthening the gradient modestly should improve that pair while keeping the last peak near or below 10 minutes.

Lowering temperature slightly from 60 C should separate the newly critical early pair, while a shorter gradient may preserve separation in the reordered middle cluster. This tests a fast compromise between the two temperature-dependent bottlenecks.
Injection 7 already achieved the maximum possible CRF. Keep it as the best method and test a slightly longer gradient for greater resolution margin while likely retaining a zero time penalty.

Injection 7 remains optimal in CRF. Slightly reducing the final organic fraction gives a slope between injections 7 and 8, testing whether the two critical pairs can both remain above 1.5 with a better minimum-resolution margin.

The maximum CRF is already secured by injection 7. Raising the starting organic fraction tests a selectivity change for the slope-insensitive critical pair, while the longer gradient aims to preserve separation of the earlier pair.

Injection 10 retained the maximum CRF with a slightly larger resolution margin. Continue the starting-solvent adjustment with a compensating increase in gradient time to test whether that margin can improve further without a time penalty.

A modestly shallower gradient should lift the early critical pair above 1.5 while preserving the middle pair’s margin. The last peak is expected before 10 minutes, offering another candidate at the maximum CRF.

Test a compromise between injection 10’s shorter retention and injection 12’s larger resolution margin. This should strengthen the early critical pair while checking whether the middle pair remains fully resolved, with no expected time penalty.

Narrow the solvent window around the observed elution range while keeping the slope close to injection 12’s successful slope. This tests a lower-organic endpoint with full resolution and a last-peak time expected just below the time-penalty threshold.

Test a slope between injections 12 and 14, where both critical pairs should retain resolution margins above 1.5 without a time penalty. The maximum CRF is already secured; this refines the range of equally scoring methods.

Slightly steepen injection 10’s gradient using a narrower solvent window to shorten retention while targeting resolution above 1.5 for both critical pairs. Previously demonstrated CRF 1.000 methods remain the benchmark.

Slightly steepen injection 16’s gradient to reduce retention while targeting full resolution of both critical pairs. The endpoint remains comfortably above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, so all compounds should elute within the gradient.

Test a slope between injections 11 and 12 to seek full resolution with a shorter retention time than injection 12. The established maximum-CRF methods remain available; this candidate targets a useful resolution margin with no time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already secured, so test a cooler selectivity regime against injection 3’s identical gradient. This will determine whether cooling separates the critical cluster more effectively than the extensively tested 55 C regime.

Return to the successful 55 C regime and test a slope between injections 10 and 13. Both critical pairs should remain above 1.5, with the last peak before 10 minutes, making this another likely maximum-CRF method.

Use a narrower solvent window with a slope close to injection 12, which achieved CRF 1.000 and a minimum resolution of 1.70. This should preserve full resolution and zero time penalty while keeping the last peak inside the gradient.

Refine between injections 18 and 21 with a slope expected to keep both critical pairs above 1.5 and the last peak below 10 minutes. This targets another maximum-CRF method with a useful resolution margin.

Trim the endpoint while preserving injection 16’s successful gradient slope; its last peak is predicted to remain inside the gradient. This tests a shorter programmed gradient expected to retain CRF 1.000.

Preserve injection 7’s successful slope while trimming its unused high-organic gradient segment. All peaks should still elute during the gradient, retaining the maximum CRF and approximately 7.60-minute last-peak time.

Use the final injection to test a slope between injections 14 and 15, targeting minimum resolution near 1.7 with no time penalty. The campaign has already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000; this candidate seeks to retain that score with additional separation margin.
